tagline: Up the North Fork to Yellowstone, past Buffalo Bill's lodge.
intro: About 25 miles west of Cody, at the edge of the Shoshone National Forest, the highway takes up the North Fork of the Shoshone River and follows it 27 paved miles up the Wapiti Valley to Yellowstone's East Entrance. The route is known for its rock formations and its wildlife.
This was the first national forest, set aside in 1891 as part of the Yellowstone Timberland Reserve. The valley's name is the Indian word for elk, and the forest keeps more than 20,000 of them.

moments.title: Wapiti Ranger Station
moments.text: On the north side of the highway is the oldest ranger station in the Forest Service, a log building of native timber put up in 1903, the first built with federal money.

moments.title: Mummy Cave
moments.text: A shallow alcove in a volcanic cliff beside the highway held 28 feet of deposits from thousands of years of visits, and an inhabitant from about AD 800 whom researchers named Mummy Joe.

moments.title: Pahaska Tepee
moments.text: Buffalo Bill marked the spot with a hand ax on a November hunt in 1901, then built a log lodge here, two miles short of Yellowstone, for tourists on the Cody Road.

practical: The byway is open year round, but Yellowstone's East Entrance closes for the season on the first Monday of November.
